points.t: Itchy, ill-defined dry or weeping patches: cheeks in infants, flexures in children and adults.
Leaky skin barrier plus Th2 inflammation, kept going by the itch–scratch cycle.
Emollient for everyone, every day. Topical steroid stepped to severity and site.
Eczema herpeticum: punched-out erosions in an unwell patient. Same-day admission.

cause.lead: A leaky barrier meets an over-reactive immune system.
points: **Barrier defect**: filaggrin-related dryness and disordered lipids → water out, irritants and allergens in.
**Th2 inflammation** drives the itch.
**Itch–scratch cycle** → lichenification and infection.
**Triggers**: soaps, detergents, *S. aureus*, allergens, heat, wool, stress.
**Contact**: irritant (dose-dependent, anyone) or allergic (type IV, needs prior sensitisation).

visuals.caption: Healthy ‘brick wall’ barrier (left) vs eczema (right): water escapes, irritants, allergens and microbes get in, and immune cells gather.
visuals.alt: Skin barrier as a brick wall, intact versus cracked

features.lead: Itch first. Then look at the pattern for the patient’s age.
points: **Acute**: red, weeping, vesicles or crust; intense itch.
**Chronic**: dry, scaly, **lichenified**, excoriated; pigment change.
**Edges are ill-defined** (psoriasis is sharp).
**Skin of colour**: redness looks violaceous or grey-brown. Judge on thickening, scale and symptoms.
**Infected?** Honey crust, pustules, rapid worsening, fever.

visuals.caption: Pattern by age: infant cheeks, scalp and outer limbs (nappy area spared); child elbow and knee creases, neck; adult hands, flexures, neck and eyelids.
visuals.alt: Infant, child and adult outlines showing typical eczema sites

items.name: Infant
items.t: Red, rough cheeks, scalp and trunk; nappy area often spared.

items.name: Adult / chronic
items.t: Lichenified, excoriated; hand and nipple eczema common.

items.name: Hand
items.t: Dry, red, scaly dorsal hands and fingers.

items.name: Irritant contact
items.t: Dry, fissured, sore skin at exposure sites.

items.name: Allergic contact
items.t: Matches the contact pattern; may spread.

Occupation, hobbies, products on the skin.
Personal or family **atopy**; sleep and quality of life.
Whole skin: excoriation, lichenification, infection.
Check nails and eyes.
Grade mild, moderate or severe on area, itch, sleep loss, exudate and thickening.
EASI / SCORAD are specialist tools.

cards.name: Psoriasis
cards.clue: Well-demarcated silvery plaques on extensors and scalp; less itchy; nail pits.

cards.name: Seborrhoeic dermatitis
cards.clue: Greasy yellow scale: scalp, nasolabial folds, eyebrows, chest.

cards.name: Tinea corporis
cards.clue: Asymmetrical annular plaque, active scaly edge; scrapings positive.

cards.name: Scabies
cards.clue: Night itch, burrows in web spaces, wrists, genitals; itchy contacts.

cards.name: Contact dermatitis
cards.clue: Matches exposure in time and place; often asymmetrical or occupational.

cards.name: Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma
cards.clue: Rare. Persistent atypical plaques in an older adult: refer.

manage.lead: Stepped care (NICE / CKS atopic eczema). Match potency to severity and site.

points: **Emollient** liberally and often; soap substitute. No aqueous cream as leave-on.
Avoid fragranced soaps, bubble baths, wool. Keep nails short.
OTC **hydrocortisone 1%** short courses, within licence.

rx.note: Face and flexures: moderate at most.

points: **Topical calcineurin inhibitors** (tacrolimus, pimecrolimus): often specialist or GPwER started.
Phototherapy or systemic treatment: refer.

limits.t: Back to emollient; ± weekend steroid on hotspots (not face, genitals, axillae without advice).
No potent steroid without specialist advice; never very potent in children.

sites.t: Not unwell: no routine antibiotic. If needed: **flucloxacillin**; clarithromycin if penicillin-allergic (erythromycin in pregnancy). Small area: consider topical fusidic acid. Replace contaminated pots.
Identify and avoid the cause; gloves (cotton liners) for wet work; short steroid course. Patch test if chronic, occupational, face or hands.
Non-sedating antihistamines do little. Short sedating course only if sleep badly disturbed.

items.t: **Eczema herpeticum**: clustered punched-out erosions or vesicles, often with fever. Hospital + aciclovir.
Severe or spreading infection, or a systemically unwell patient.
Severe disease not controlled after about a week of stepped treatment.
Diagnostic doubt, recurrent deep infections, major psychosocial impact.
Possible phototherapy or systemics; occupational disease needing workplace advice.

pearls.t: **Prescribe enough emollient**: adults often need several hundred grams a month.
**Fire risk**: emollient-soaked fabrics burn easily. Keep away from flames.
Teach **fingertip units** so steroid doses make sense.
Tackle **steroid phobia**: under-treatment harms more often than steroids do.
**Inflamed ≠ infected**: weeping crust does not automatically mean an antibiotic.
Not caused by poor hygiene; the barrier tendency is lifelong.

quiz.q: How long should a topical steroid continue after a flare?
quiz.a: About 48 hours after the flare settles, then back to emollient maintenance.

quiz.q: First-line oral antibiotic for infected eczema, if one is needed?
quiz.a: Flucloxacillin (clarithromycin if penicillin-allergic; erythromycin if pregnant and allergic).

quiz.q: What suggests eczema herpeticum, and what do you do?
quiz.a: Clustered punched-out erosions or vesicles, often with fever. Same-day hospital assessment and aciclovir.
Under-prescribing emollient: adults often need several hundred grams a month.
